summary:
We developed FireAtlas, an interactive website that brings NASA FIRMS fire hotspot observations from MODIS and VIIRS together on a single map. Users can select an area and date range, explore daily activity and seasonal trends and compare original satellite observations with an adjusted historical record for Malaysia from 2003 to 2023.

MODIS and VIIRS have different detection capabilities, so switching sensors can change the number of hotspots recorded even when fire activity stays similar. FireAtlas addresses this challenge by adjusting the historical record to a common scale and clearly labeling observed detections and model estimates. Users can also click an observed hotspot to search for news from the surrounding area within three days of the latest detection.

FireAtlas makes satellite fire data easier to interpret across years. It helps users spot seasonal peaks and unusually active periods while accounting for differences between sensors.
details:
What FireAtlas does

FireAtlas is an interactive web application that helps users explore satellite fire hotspot observations from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). Users can select a region, draw a custom area on a 3D globe, and filter observations by date. Clicking a day on the activity calendar updates the map, making it easier to see where hotspots were detected during unusually active periods.

How it works

MODIS and VIIRS differ in their ability to detect hotspots, so a shift in recorded counts can reflect a change in sensors as well as a change in fire activity. FireAtlas lets users compare the original satellite records with adjusted trends. For Malaysia’s 2003–2020 historical record, we used the overlap between Aqua MODIS and Suomi NPP VIIRS to estimate earlier activity on a VIIRS-equivalent scale. The application labels observed detections, model estimates, and simulated locations so users can tell which type of data they are viewing.

Benefits and intended impact

FireAtlas makes satellite fire data easier to explore without manually processing separate files. Students, researchers, and people interested in local fire activity can use it to identify seasonal peaks, investigate unusually active months, and compare patterns across years. Our goal is to help users make more informed comparisons when the underlying satellite instruments change.

Tools and technologies

We built the interface with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, and used MapLibre GL JS for the interactive globe. We used Python and pandas for data processing, DuckDB and Parquet for storing and querying observations, and FastAPI for the backend. The project uses existing satellite observations and runs on standard computers with a WebGL-capable browser.

Creativity and design considerations

We linked the map, activity calendar, and trend charts so users can move from a long-term pattern to the locations behind a particular day’s readings. We also added a news search to observed hotspot popups. It uses an editable place name and searches within three days of the latest detection, giving users a starting point for exploring local reports. The popup explains that nearby news may be unrelated to the detection.

Our team considered sensor differences, the clarity of the map and charts, and the uncertainty in the adjusted historical record. The delivered Malaysia model fell short of the target of 15% monthly error or less, so we include validation results and keep the original observations available alongside the adjusted series.
